lessons.title: What is a makhraj?
body: A makhraj is the place a letter's sound comes from. Every letter of the Arabic alphabet has its own; producing each letter from the right place is the first step of tajweed.

The makhraj fall into five areas: the jawf (the open space of the mouth and throat), the halq (throat), the tongue, the lips and the khayshum (nasal cavity). By the best-known count of the scholars there are 17 in all: 1 in the jawf, 3 in the throat, 10 on the tongue, 2 at the lips and 1 in the nose.
The next lessons go through each area in turn. To find a letter's makhraj, say it with a sukun after a hamza with a vowel (for example «ab», «at»): where the sound stops is that letter's makhraj.

lessons.title: Throat letters
body: Six letters come from the throat, from three makhraj:
• The deepest part of the throat (near the chest): ء (hamza) and ه (ha). • The middle of the throat: ع (ʿayn) and ح (ḥa). • The top of the throat (near the mouth): غ (ghayn) and خ (kha).
Many languages lack some of these sounds, so take care to tell ح from ه and ع from hamza. ح comes from the middle of the throat: a breathy sound with no voice, but with a strong stream of air.

lessons.title: Tongue letters
body: Eighteen letters come from the tongue, the largest area. The main groups:

• The back of the tongue against the soft palate: ق (qaf); a little further forward: ك (kaf).
• The middle of the tongue against the palate: ج, ش and ي when it has a vowel or is not a madd letter.
• The side of the tongue against the upper molars: ض.
• The front of the tongue: ل, ن, ر, each from a slightly different place.
• The tip of the tongue against the roots of the upper front teeth: ت, د, ط.
• The tip of the tongue near the front teeth, with a whistle: ص, س, ز.
• The tip of the tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth: ث, ذ, ظ.
The most common mistakes are saying ق like ك, ض like د or ظ, and ث like س. Practise the letters one by one with a sukun.

lessons.title: Lip letters
body: Four letters come from the lips, from two makhraj:

• ف: the inside of the lower lip touches the edges of the upper front teeth. • ب, م and و (when it has a vowel or is not a madd letter): both lips. For ب and م the lips close; for و they round and do not close fully.
Don't say و like an English «v», with the teeth on the lip: the teeth play no part in the Arabic و.

lessons.title: The jawf and the khayshum
body: The jawf is the open space of the mouth and throat. The three madd letters come from it: a silent ا after a fatha, a silent و after a damma and a silent ي after a kasra. They last as long as the air does, so they have no single point.
The khayshum is the nasal cavity. The ghunna comes from here: the nasal sound that goes with nun and mim. Pinch your nose and the ghunna stops, which shows it comes from the khayshum.

lessons.title: Fatha, kasra, damma and sukun
body: The vowel marks show which vowel a letter is read with:

• Fatha (a slanted stroke above the letter, ـَ): the «a» sound. • Kasra (a slanted stroke below the letter, ـِ): the «i» sound. • Damma (a small waw above the letter, ـُ): the «u» sound. • Sukun (a small circle above the letter, ـْ): the letter has no vowel and is said short and clean.
These vowels are short: one count each. Stretching them goes against the rules of madd and can change the meaning.

lessons.title: Tashdid (shadda)
body: A tashdid (ـّ) means the letter is said twice: first silent, then with its vowel. In رَبِّ, for example, the ب is said twice: «rab-bi».
Hold the doubled letter for a moment, then say it with its vowel. Dropping a tashdid can change a word's meaning, so watch for it. A doubled nun or mim is said with ghunna (see the Ghunna lesson).

lessons.title: Tanwin
body: Tanwin is a doubled vowel mark at the end of a word (ـً ـٍ ـٌ). It stands for a silent nun that is pronounced but not written: «-an», «-in», «-un».
Depending on the letter after it, this nun is said clearly, hidden, or merged into the next letter; those rules are in the section «Nun sakin and tanwin».
When stopping (waqf) on a fatha tanwin, it becomes a long «a»; when stopping on a kasra or damma tanwin, the letter ends with a sukun.

lessons.title: Natural madd
body: Madd is stretching a sound. There are three madd letters: a silent ا after a fatha, a silent و after a damma and a silent ي after a kasra.
When no hamza or sukun follows the madd letter, it is a natural madd, stretched two counts: twice a short vowel. Cutting it short and stretching it too far are both mistakes.
Listen to the marked places in the examples and match the length to the reciter's.

lessons.title: Connected madd (muttasil)
body: When a hamza follows a madd letter in the same word, it is a connected (muttasil) madd. In the Hafs narration it is stretched 4 or 5 counts and never shortened, which is why it is also called the «obligatory madd».
For example: جَآءَ, ٱلسَّمَآءِ. Keep the length you choose (4 or 5) the same throughout a recitation.

lessons.title: Separated madd (munfasil)
body: When a madd letter ends a word and a hamza starts the next word, it is a separated (munfasil) madd. In the Hafs narration, by the best-known way, it is stretched 4 or 5 counts.
For example: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا, إِنَّآ أَعْطَيْنَـٰكَ. The difference from the connected madd: the hamza is in another word.

lessons.title: Necessary madd (lazim)
body: When a madd letter is followed in the same word by a permanent sukun or a shadda, it is a necessary (lazim) madd, always stretched 6 counts.
The best-known example is ٱلضَّآلِّينَ at the end of al-Fatiha. The separate letters that open some surahs also have it (for example the «lam» and «mim» of الٓمٓ).

lessons.title: Madd when stopping, and lin
body: When you stop (waqf) at the end of an ayah or a word, the letter after a madd letter becomes silent because of the stop. This makes a temporary (ʿarid) madd, which may be stretched 2, 4 or 6 counts. For example, stopping on ٱلْعَـٰلَمِينَ.
Lin madd: stopping after a silent و or ي that follows a fatha, as in خَوْفٍ, ٱلْبَيْتِ. It is also 2, 4 or 6 counts. When you read on without stopping, these are not stretched.

lessons.title: Izhar (clear)
body: When one of the throat letters (ء ه ع ح غ خ) follows a nun sakin (نْ) or tanwin, the nun is said clearly, with no ghunna. This is izhar (making clear).
The reason: the throat letters come from far from the nun, so the two sounds don't merge. For example: أَنْعَمْتَ (al-Fatiha, ayah 7), مِّنْ خَوْفٍ, كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ.

lessons.title: Idgham (merging)
body: When one of the letters ي ر م ل و ن follows a nun sakin or tanwin, the nun merges into the next letter: this is idgham. The word «yarmalun» (يَرْمَلُونَ) helps to remember them.
• Idgham with ghunna: with ي ن م و, the merge carries a ghunna of two counts. • Idgham without ghunna: with ل and ر, the nun disappears completely, with no ghunna.
Idgham only happens between two words. When the nun and one of these letters are in the same word (for example دُنْيَا), the nun is said clearly.

lessons.title: Iqlab (turning)
body: When ب follows a nun sakin or tanwin, the nun turns into a mim sound, said with ghunna and lightly closed lips. This is iqlab (turning).
The mushaf marks these places with a small mim (ۢ or ۭ) over the nun or tanwin: the sign of iqlab. For example: مِنۢ بَعْدِ, كِرَامٍۭ بَرَرَةٍ.

lessons.title: Ikhfa (hiding)
body: When one of the remaining 15 letters (ص ذ ث ك ج ش ق س د ط ز ف ت ض ظ) follows a nun sakin or tanwin, the nun is hidden and said with ghunna. This is ikhfa.

Ikhfa sits between izhar and idgham: the nun is neither fully clear nor fully merged. The tongue doesn't touch the nun's place; the sound comes through the nose as ghunna while the mouth gets ready for the next letter. The ghunna lasts two counts.

lessons.title: Lip ikhfa (shafawi)
body: When ب follows a mim sakin (مْ), the mim is hidden with lightly closed lips and a ghunna. This is lip (shafawi) ikhfa, because both letters come from the lips.
For example: تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ (surah al-Fil). The ghunna lasts two counts.

lessons.title: Lip idgham (shafawi)
body: When another mim follows a mim sakin, the two become one doubled mim, said with ghunna. This is lip idgham (the idgham of two identical letters).
For example: لَهُم مَّا. The ghunna lasts two counts.

lessons.title: Lip izhar (shafawi)
body: When any letter other than ب and م follows a mim sakin, the mim is said clearly, with no ghunna. This is lip izhar.
Take special care before و and ف: they also come from near the lips, so it is easy to hide the mim by mistake. For example: عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ, أَلَمْ تَرَ, هُمْ فِيهَا.

lessons.title: Ghunna
body: Ghunna is the sound that comes from the nasal cavity. It is part of every nun and mim.
It is at its fullest in a doubled nun (نّ) and a doubled mim (مّ), where it is held for two counts. For example: إِنَّ, ثُمَّ, ٱلنَّاسِ. Don't rush over these letters.

lessons.title: Qalqala (echo)
body: There are five qalqala letters: ق ط ب ج د. The phrase «qutbu jad» (قُطْبُ جَدٍّ) helps to remember them.

When these letters have a sukun, they get a slight echo, a bounce, as they leave their makhraj. In the middle of a word the qalqala is light; when stopping at the end of an ayah it is stronger. For example: stopping on ٱلصَّمَدُ, and يَخْلُقْ.
Don't turn the qalqala into a vowel: it isn't an «a», «i» or «u», only a short bounce.

lessons.title: Sun and moon lam, and the connecting hamza
body: The lam of the article ال is read in two ways:

• Moon lam (qamariyya): said clearly. The letters after it are gathered in the phrase «ابغ حجك وخف عقيمه»: ٱلْقَمَرُ, ٱلْحَمْدُ. • Sun lam (shamsiyya): not said, and the next letter is doubled. The other 14 letters: ٱلشَّمْسُ, ٱلرَّحْمَـٰنِ, ٱلنَّاسِ.

The connecting hamza (ٱ) is only said when you start from that word; when it is joined to the word before, it falls silent. The mushaf also has letters that are written but not read; the examples mark them.

lessons.title: Idgham of kindred and close letters
body: When a silent letter is followed by a letter from the same makhraj but with different qualities, the first merges into the second: this is the idgham of kindred letters (mutajanisayn). For example: قَد تَّبَيَّنَ (د into ت), إِذ ظَّلَمُوٓا۟.
When two letters from nearby makhraj meet, it is the idgham of close letters (mutaqaribayn). For example: أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّم (ق into ك), قُل رَّبِّ.
These cases are rare in the Qur'an, so watch for the shadda sign in the mushaf.

lessons.title: The letter ra and the word «Allah»
body: Ra (ر) is said in two ways: • Heavy (tafkhim): with a fatha or damma, or when silent after a fatha or damma: رَبِّ, قُرْءَانٌ. • Light (tarqiq): with a kasra, or when silent after a kasra (and no heavy letter follows): رِجَالٌ, فِرْعَوْنَ.
The lam in the word «Allah» is heavy after a fatha or damma (قُلْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ, شَهِدَ ٱللَّهُ) and light after a kasra (بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ, لِلَّهِ).

lessons.title: Stopping signs (waqf)
body: The mushaf has signs inside the ayahs that show where you may stop (waqf):

• مـ: you must stop; reading on could spoil the meaning. • لا: don't stop here. • ج: stopping and reading on are both allowed. • صلى: reading on is better. • قلى: stopping is better. • ∴ ∴ (two sets of three dots): stop at only one of the two places.
When you stop, the word ends with a sukun (except a fatha tanwin). If your breath runs out, stop at a suitable place and go back a word or two.
